hints: Notice the question asks for the volt, the unit of potential difference $V$, and the options mix coulombs for charge, joules for energy and seconds for time.
Connect potential difference to energy transferred per charge moved using $V = W/Q$, with $W$ in joules and $Q$ in coulombs.
Compare each option to that ratio and to the familiar $I = Q/t$ for current and $P = W/t$ for power to eliminate the coulomb per second and joule per second distractors.
walkthrough: Identify what one volt measures: potential difference $V$ between two points, defined as work done per unit charge moved.
State the governing relation $V = W/Q$, where $W$ is energy in joules $\text{J}$ and $Q$ is charge in coulombs $\text{C}$.
Put units into the relation: unit of $V$ = unit of $W$ divided by unit of $Q$, so $1 \text{ V} = 1 \text{ J} / 1 \text{ C}$.
Check the distractors: one coulomb per second is $Q/t$, the ampere, and one joule per second is $W/t$, the watt.
Therefore one volt is equivalent to one joule per coulomb. This is option B.

options.A: One coulomb per second is charge flow rate, which defines the ampere for current $I = Q/t$, not the volt.
options.B: Potential difference is energy per unit charge $V = W/Q$, so $1 \text{ V} = 1 \text{ J C}^{-1}$.
options.C: One joule per second is energy transfer rate, which defines the watt for power $P = W/t$, not the volt.
options.D: Joule second per coulomb squared does not match $W/Q$ and has no meaning as a simple SI electrical unit here.
